summary:
Field Analog Atlas is a data-backed prototype for comparing Earth landscapes with candidate exploration areas on the Moon and Mars.
It uses topology data (terrain, mean slope, elevation) to compare three Earth sites Harrat Khaybar, Lake Magadi, and the Makgadikgadi Pans with Slater Plain near the lunar south pole and Jezero crater on Mars. The interactive web app presents the candidate locations on an Earth globe, shows exploratory similarity scores and the terrain factors behind them, and provides separate globes and landscape comparisons for the lunar and Martian targets. The prototype addresses the challenge of finding places on Earth that could help prepare astronauts and evaluate equipment for future missions.
details:
Project details

Galactic Star Guide: Field Analog Atlas is a research prototype for comparing Earth landscapes with selected exploration regions on the Moon and Mars. It helps users explore which places may be useful analogs for astronaut field training or equipment trials, while showing both the evidence for a match and the limits of that comparison.

What it does and how it works

The prototype compares three Earth candidates; Harrat Khaybar in Saudi Arabia, Lake Magadi in Kenya, and the Makgadikgadi Pans in Botswana with Slater Plain near the lunar south pole and Jezero crater on Mars.

Its current comparison uses three terrain measures: local relief, mean slope, and neighborhood elevation variability. Python scripts summarize and compare the terrain data, then calculate an exploratory similarity score for each Earth site against each target. The website displays those scores, the underlying measurements, and written summaries of where a candidate resembles or differs from the target. Interactive globes show the candidate and target locations, with landscape and orbital terrain imagery for context.

This is not yet a trained machine-learning model. The scores are transparent, exploratory terrain (topology) comparisons based on a small set of preselected locations. Factors such as mineralogy, temperature, dust, and operational hazards have not yet been included in the scores.

Benefits and intended impact

The atlas makes planetary analog research easier to inspect: users can see how a score was produced instead of relying on a single unexplained ranking. It can help researchers identify candidate field sites, plan future terrain or equipment studies, and decide which additional data would improve a comparison. The intended impact is better-informed preparation for human exploration, not a claim that any Earth site fully reproduces the Moon or Mars.

Tools and technology

  • Data and analysis: NASA SRTM elevation data for Earth, LOLA elevation data for the Moon, and MOLA elevation data for Mars.
  • Analysis code: Python, using NumPy, Rasterio, PyShp, and Pillow, alongside Python’s standard library.
  • Interactive website: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js for the rotatable globes.
  • Hardware: Developed on a standard desktop computer; no specialized hardware was required.

What makes it creative

The project brings together terrain analysis, planetary science, and an interactive atlas so people can explore cross-world comparisons visually and examine the reasoning behind them. Its approach also treats mismatches and missing evidence as part of the experience: users can see not only what appears similar, but also what the current data cannot establish.
